proofs.proof_tex:
By the design-A nonemptiness criterion,
\[
 \mathcal F_A(p,m)\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 m\in\Delta_{\mathcal E}^{\circ}
 \ \text{and}\ 
 \mathcal C_A(T)\ne\varnothing . \tag{15}
\]
Thus the strict-interior margin test is necessary even if the normalized cycle
fiber is nonempty.  For design B, surjectivity in the cycle-to-SCM lift gives
\[
 \mathcal F_B(p)\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal C_B(T)\ne\varnothing . \tag{16}
\]
An empty fiber has an empty target image and hence cardinality zero, rather
than one.  Therefore failure of either applicable test is correctly reported
as incompatibility and is non-rigid according to PN/PS rigidity.

Suppose next that the relevant full fiber is nonempty.  The same lift lemma is
onto and preserves the causal target, so
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathcal T_A(p,m)
 &=\{\tau_C(b,a):(b,a)\in\mathcal C_A(T)\},\\
 \mathcal T_B(p)
 &=\{\tau_C(b,a):(b,a,m,g,\pi)\in\mathcal C_B(T)\}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{17}
\]
The mixed-support elimination theorem writes either cycle fiber in (17) as a
finite union \(X=\bigcup_{\chi}X_{\chi}\) of its structural charts.  Its
one-sample/all-chart conclusion supplies \(x_0\in X\), puts
\(t_0=\tau_C(x_0)\), and proves
\[
 \tau_C(X)=\{t_0\}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 X_{\chi}\cap
 \left\{x:\|\tau_C(x)-t_0\|_2^2>0\right\}=\varnothing
 \quad\text{for every }\chi . \tag{18}
\]
This is a comparison with the same \(t_0\) on every chart, so (18) also
compares disconnected components and distinct support faces.  Combining
(17)--(18) proves the asserted necessary-and-sufficient rigidity tests.

The mixed-support theorem also establishes the stated output discipline over
\(\mathbb K_{\zeta}\): a field expression is returned only when constructed;
otherwise the selected coordinate is represented by a square-free
real-univariate polynomial, rational coordinate functions, and Thom signs.
For rational input, clearing guarded denominators and isolating the selected
real root gives the stated integer-polynomial and rational-isolating-interval
form.

If a refinement in (18) is nonempty, its sampled point \(x_1\) satisfies
\(\tau_C(x_1)\ne\tau_C(x_0)\).  Both points are in the same observable cycle
fiber.  Applying the cycle-to-SCM lift separately gives two legal full SCMs
with the same selected law and, in design A, the same supplied margin vector,
while target preservation gives unequal values of \(\tau\).  If both sampled
points belong to interior support charts, the interior positive-lift lemma
makes every response mass, proxy and instrument kernel, treatment probability,
and selection probability strictly interior.  That lemma has no such
conclusion when either point is on a support face, which proves exactly the
boundary qualification in the statement.  No connected-component
description was used in any implication.

Condition 1 of Shingaki--Yoshida--Kuroki has the selected-law factorization
\[
 p(x,y,s,w,z,u)
 =p(s\mid x,y)p(y\mid x,u)p(x\mid z,u)
   p(w\mid u)p(z\mid u)p(u). \tag{19}
\]
In the present model, response consistency makes \(p(y\mid x,u)\) the
deterministic kernel encoded by the four response types.  Outcome-dependent
selection supplies \(p(s\mid x,y)\), proxy exclusion supplies
\(p(w\mid u)\), and the definitions of the treatment, second-proxy, and
response-type mechanisms supply the remaining factors.  Thus, at this
factorization level, \(\mathfrak M\) is precisely the finite four-response-type
specialization of Condition 1.

The design-A definition adds
\[
 P_{\vartheta}(E,W,Z\mid S=1)=p,
 \qquad P_{\vartheta}(E)=m. \tag{20}
\]
Consequently \(\mathcal F_A(p,m)\) is the subfiber obtained by fixing the
population cell margins.  On a compatible member satisfying the published
regular Conditions 2--3, the cited regular-identification lemma applies
pointwise.  If \(R_A(p)\) denotes the pair computed by Appendix equations
(A.28)--(A.33), it gives
\[
 \tau(\vartheta)=R_A(p)
 \quad\text{for every }\vartheta\in\mathcal F_A(p,m). \tag{21}
\]
Compatibility makes this fiber nonempty, so
\[
 \mathcal T_A(p,m)=\{R_A(p)\}. \tag{22}
\]
The full-rigidity theorem returns the unique element of this target set;
hence the returned value is the published one.  This is transfer by
restriction: fixing \(m\) does not weaken a conclusion already valid for
every member of the larger regular fiber.

For design B, instrument exogeneity changes the final two factors of (19) to
\(p(z\mid u)p(u)=g(z)p(u)\).  Hence every member obeys
\[
 p(x,y,s,w,z,u)
 =p(s\mid x,y)p(y\mid x,u)p(x\mid z,u)
   p(w\mid u)g(z)p(u), \tag{23}
\]
which is equation (13) of the cited paper.  The definition of
\(\mathcal F_B(p)\) additionally imposes the displayed instrument-relevance
inequality.  On a compatible law satisfying Conditions 2--3, the cited
regular IV identification result applies directly to (23).  Writing its
observable answer as \(R_B(p)\),
\[
 \tau(\vartheta)=R_B(p)
 \quad\text{for every }\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p),
 \qquad
 \mathcal T_B(p)=\{R_B(p)\}. \tag{24}
\]
The full-rigidity theorem again forces the compiler to return this unique
value.

Neither (21) nor (24) is invoked outside the published regular conditions.
There the mixed-support theorem exhausts rank-two orientations, rank-one
\(\mathrm L,\mathrm R,\mathrm E,\mathrm D\) modes, all coefficient-support
faces, shared endpoints, and, in design B, all residual-forest and active-cycle
states.  The full-rigidity theorem consequently returns either the common
exact target or legal target-changing SCM lifts on every compatible singular
or boundary law, while (15)--(16) of its proof distinguish incompatibility.
This proves a compatible singular/boundary classification extension only; it
neither enlarges the domain of the published regular formula nor asserts
blanket subsumption.

On the stated experimental submodel, \(S=1\) almost surely implies
\(m=r\), and \(X\perp(U,W,Z)\) implies
\(P(U=i\mid X=x)=\pi_i\).  The cited experimental identification lemma says
that Conditions (1)--(3) identify the four response-type probabilities and
that its equations (8)--(13) give a consistent plug-in estimator.  We first
show that these observable conditions also make the larger design-A cycle
fiber target-rigid.

Fix a cell \(e=(x,y)\) with incident response types \(i,j\).  For a proxy
category \(w\), define the cell-conditional matrix
\[
 \widetilde Q_{ew}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&P(W=w\mid E=e)\\
 P(Z=z_1\mid E=e)&P(W=w,Z=z_1\mid E=e)
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The matrix \(Q_{xyw}\) in the cited construction differs only by the positive
cell-probability normalizations, so its relevant determinant vanishes exactly
when \(\det(\widetilde Q_{ew})\) vanishes.
Substituting
\(T_e=b_i a_{ei}^{\top}+b_j a_{ej}^{\top}\) and expanding the two products
gives
\[
 \det(\widetilde Q_{ew})=K_e\{b_i(w)-b_j(w)\}, \tag{25}
\]
where, on writing \(A_{ei}=\sum_z a_{ei}(z)\) and
\(A_{ej}=\sum_z a_{ej}(z)\),
\[
 K_e=a_{ei}(z_1)A_{ej}-A_{ei}a_{ej}(z_1),
\]
which does not depend on \(w\).  Condition (3) makes the determinant contrast
used by the cited equations nonzero, so \(K_e\ne0\) and \(b_i\ne b_j\).
Thus the determinant ratios are observable direction ratios for
\(\mathcal L_e\), and each \(T_e\) has rank two.  The four separation
inequalities in Condition (3) make the two incident directions used for each
response type distinct.  The nonsingular \(2\)-by-\(2\) systems in equations
(8)--(11) therefore identify the unique intersection of its two incident
lines, namely the common endpoint \(b_i\).

The rank-two orientation atlas is exhaustive.  Once every shared endpoint is
the unique incident-line intersection just obtained, every nonempty oriented
endpoint interval is a singleton.  Formula
\[
 a_{ei}(z)
 =v_e(z)
 \frac{c_{ez}(h)-b_j(h)}{b_i(h)-b_j(h)},
 \qquad c_{ez}=T_e(\cdot,z)/v_e(z), \tag{26}
\]
for any separating coordinate \(h\), then uniquely fixes the coefficient
rows as well.  Hence the whole cycle fiber has one target value, equal to the
value of the generating experimental SCM.

Under the label conversion
\(\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}=(\pi_4,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_1)\), response consistency and
randomization give
\[
 \mathrm{PN}
 =\frac{\pi_2}{\pi_1+\pi_2}
 =\frac{\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}_2}
        {\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}_2+\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}_4},
 \qquad
 \mathrm{PS}
 =\frac{\pi_2}{\pi_2+\pi_4}
 =\frac{\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}_2}
        {\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}_1+\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}_2}. \tag{27}
\]
Positive observed cells make both denominators positive.  Equations
(25)--(27), the cycle-to-SCM lift, and the rank-two atlas prove
\[
 \mathcal T_A(p,r)
 =\{\phi_{\mathrm{SK}}(\pi^{\mathrm{SK}})\}. \tag{28}
\]
The all-rank-two branch occurs among the charts enumerated by
\(\mathscr A\), so the exact compiler returns the same singleton.  The cited
plug-in consistency and continuity of \(\phi_{\mathrm{SK}}\) at the positive
denominators in (27) yield
\[
 \phi_{\mathrm{SK}}(\widehat\pi_n^{\mathrm{SK}})
 \xrightarrow{P}\phi_{\mathrm{SK}}(\pi^{\mathrm{SK}}). \tag{29}
\]

We now verify the boundary datum without a genericity argument.  Each listed
\(b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}\) is strictly positive and has coordinates summing to
one.  In every cell the two displayed coefficient rows are nonnegative, their
coordinatewise sum is \((1/3,1/3,1/3)\), and they are not proportional.  The
two incident endpoint vectors are distinct.  Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(T_e^{\mathrm{bd}})=2
 \quad\text{for every }e. \tag{30}
\]
For every \((w,z)\), at least one incident coefficient is positive, while all
endpoint coordinates are positive; hence every entry of
\(T_e^{\mathrm{bd}}\), and then every entry of \(p^{\mathrm{bd}}\), is
positive.  Moreover
\[
 \sum_e s_e^{\mathrm{bd}}m_e^{\mathrm{bd}}
 =\frac14\left(\frac18+\frac14+\frac38+\frac12\right)
 =\frac5{16},
 \qquad
 \frac{s_e^{\mathrm{bd}}m_e^{\mathrm{bd}}}{5/16}
 =r_e^{\mathrm{bd}} \tag{31}
\]
cell by cell.  Thus the displayed cycle point and selection law satisfy the
normalization required by the cycle-to-SCM lift, which proves
\(\mathcal F_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\ne\varnothing\).

In simplex coordinates, direct substitution gives
\[
 \mathcal L_{11}=\mathcal L_{00}
 =\{b:b(w_2)=1/5\},\qquad
 \mathcal L_{01}=\{b:b(w_1)=1/5\},\qquad
 \mathcal L_{10}=\{b:b(w_3)=1/5\}. \tag{32}
\]
The transverse intersections in (32) pin
\(b_1^{\mathrm{bd}},b_3^{\mathrm{bd}},b_4^{\mathrm{bd}}\).  In cell \(11\),
the normalized columns at \(z_1,z_3\) are respectively
\(b_1^{\mathrm{bd}},b_2^{\mathrm{bd}}\); hence the segment constraint puts
the type-\(2\) endpoint on the ray beginning at \(b_2^{\mathrm{bd}}\) and
pointing away from \(b_1^{\mathrm{bd}}\).  In cell \(00\), the corresponding
columns are \(b_2^{\mathrm{bd}},b_4^{\mathrm{bd}}\); hence the same endpoint
lies on the ray beginning at \(b_2^{\mathrm{bd}}\) and pointing away from
\(b_4^{\mathrm{bd}}\).  Since the strict order on the common line is
\(b_1^{\mathrm{bd}},b_2^{\mathrm{bd}},b_4^{\mathrm{bd}}\), the two rays meet
only at \(b_2^{\mathrm{bd}}\).  All endpoints are fixed, and (26) fixes every
coefficient.  In particular the four displayed zeros are compulsory and
\[
 \tau_C
 =\left(0+\frac16+\frac13,
          \frac13+\frac16+0\right)
 =\left(\frac12,\frac12\right). \tag{33}
\]
The rank-two atlas and the target-preserving lift prove the asserted
singleton full-SCM target set.

On the relative support face preserving the four zeros, the exposed columns
continue to identify the relevant endpoints.  Positivity of every other
coefficient and endpoint, the strict endpoint order, transversality of the
remaining incident lines, and \(m\ne r\) are strict relative inequalities.
The displayed datum satisfies all of them, so this relative-open chart is
nonempty; the same intersection and ray argument proves its rigidity.
Finally \(r^{\mathrm{bd}}\ne m^{\mathrm{bd}}\), whereas \(S=1\) almost
surely would imply \(P(E\mid S=1)=P(E)\), hence \(r=m\).  The boundary datum
therefore lies outside the experimental conditions.

Fix \(\vartheta\in\mathcal F_B(p)\) in the stated no-selection overlap and
suppose \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}(P_{\vartheta})\).  The cited Kawakami
identification lemma applies because the factorization, invertibilities,
cross-treatment separation, and structural exclusion conditions are exactly
those recorded by \(\mathcal K_{\mathrm K}\).  It identifies the two
treatment-conditional response-type vectors \(\omega_0^{\mathrm K}\) and
\(\omega_1^{\mathrm K}\) by the simultaneous equations in the proof of its
Theorem 1.

In the order \((00,01,10,11)\), response consistency implies that
\((X,Y)=(1,1)\) admits exactly types \(01\) and \(11\), while
\((X,Y)=(0,0)\) admits exactly types \(00\) and \(01\).  The positive
selected cells and \(S=1\) almost surely make both conditioning events have
positive probability.  Therefore Bayes' rule gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathrm{PN}(\vartheta)
 &=\frac{\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,2}}
         {\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,2}+\omega^{\mathrm K}_{1,4}},\\
 \mathrm{PS}(\vartheta)
 &=\frac{\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,2}}
         {\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,1}+\omega^{\mathrm K}_{0,2}}.
 \end{aligned} \tag{34}
\]
By the definition of \(\phi_{\mathrm K}\), equation (34) is
\[
 \tau(\vartheta)
 =\phi_{\mathrm K}(\omega_0^{\mathrm K},\omega_1^{\mathrm K}). \tag{35}
\]
If \(\mathcal T_B(p)\) is a singleton, it contains \(\tau(\vartheta)\) by
definition.  The full-rigidity theorem makes the atlas return that unique
element, and hence (35).  The cited result identifies all four binary
potential-outcome-type probabilities and the conditional weights appearing
in (34); this establishes the stated description of its scope.

For the separate scope witness, every row of
\(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) has the form
\[
 \bigl(1,b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_1),
          b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_2),b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}(w_3)\bigr). \tag{36}
\]
Since \(b_i^{\mathrm{bd}}\) is a probability vector on three points, the
last three entries of (36) sum to one.  Thus, for each \(x\), the first
column of \(A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})\) is the sum of its last three
columns, and
\[
 \det A_x^{\mathrm K}(b^{\mathrm{bd}})=0. \tag{37}
\]
The experimental-overlap and boundary-separation theorem has already proved
\[
 \mathcal F_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})\ne\varnothing,
 \qquad
 \mathcal T_A(p^{\mathrm{bd}},m^{\mathrm{bd}})
 =\{(1/2,1/2)\}. \tag{38}
\]
Consequently this legal selected response-cycle law is exactly classified by
the atlas, but (37) violates the named invertibility premise in Kawakami's
Theorem 1(i).  This single-law witness proves strict scope separation; it does
not assert that either result subsumes the other.

Put \(k=|\mathcal Z|\) and \(\ell=|\mathcal W|\).  A proxy endpoint has a
nonempty support and hence at most \(2^{\ell}-1\) labeled support patterns.
The four shared response vertices contribute at most
\[
 (2^{\ell}-1)^4. \tag{39}
\]
At a rank-two cell there are two endpoint orientations.  For each of the
\(k\) values of \(z\), positivity of \(v_e(z)\) and
\(a_{ei}(z)+a_{ej}(z)=v_e(z)\) leave exactly the three coarse support states
``left zero'', ``right zero'', and ``both positive''.  Rank two therefore
contributes at most \(2\cdot3^k\) templates.  By the rank-one normal-form
lemma, mode \(\mathrm E\) contributes \(3^k\) coordinatewise split faces,
and modes \(\mathrm L,\mathrm R,\mathrm D\) add three.  Thus either positive
table rank contributes at most
\[
 2\cdot3^k+3^k+3=3^{k+1}+3 \tag{40}
\]
local templates per cell.  Multiplying (39) by the fourth power of (40)
proves the displayed value of \(M_A\).

For design B, each of the four response links is zero-residual or active.  An
active link records one of \(k-1\) first nonbaseline pivots and one of two
pivot signs, so it has
\[
 1+2(k-1)=2k-1 \tag{41}
\]
coarse states.  A relevance certificate chooses an unordered pair of
distinct instrument values and the sign of its nonzero cross-product, giving
\[
 2\binom{k}{2}=k(k-1) \tag{42}
\]
possibilities.  Exhaustiveness of the residual-forest refinement permits
multiplication of these finite labels.  Hence
\(M_B=M_Ak(k-1)(2k-1)^4\), and summing the two design counts gives
\(M_{k,\ell}=M_A+M_B\).

We next verify the uniform formula format.  Four endpoint vectors require
\(4\ell\) coordinates and the two incident coefficient vectors in four
cells require \(8k\).  In design B, projective common-instrument and joint
treatment auxiliaries require at most \(2k\) further coordinates.  Margins,
response masses, component scales, and four transfer scalars require at most
twelve more.  This proves the variable bound
\(N_0=4\ell+10k+12\).

There are \(4k\ell\) factorization equations.  Endpoint simplex and support
conditions use at most \(4\ell+4\) atoms; coefficient simplex, support, and
split conditions at most \(24k+8\); residual definitions and transfer
equations at most \(16k+8\); and all proportionality minors at most
\(4(k-1)^2\).  Shared-instrument equations, normalizations, endpoint
incidences, cycle consistency, and signed relevance use fewer than
\(20(k\ell+k^2+\ell+1)\) further atoms.  Since \(k\ge2\) and \(\ell\ge3\),
their sum is bounded by
\[
 S_0=100(k\ell+k^2+\ell+1). \tag{43}
\]
The factorization and shared-instrument equations have degree at most two.
Each residual has degree at most two, transfer-scalar proportionality has
degree at most three, the four-link cycle product has degree four, and signed
relevance has degree at most three after substitution of \(q^X\).  All other
atoms have no greater degree.  Hence \(D_0=4\).  The target is linear, so the
one added squared unequal-target atom has degree two and does not change this
bound.  This proves the format claims in (25)--(26) of the statement.

Apply the effective sampling result to each chart over
\(\mathbb K_{\zeta}\).  At most \(A_S\) records are generated per initial
chart.  If the union is nonempty, choose the first returned sample \(x_0\)
and let \(t_0=\tau_C(x_0)\).  If \(\xi\) is a primitive element for its
real-univariate representation, then
\[
 [\mathbb K_{\zeta}(\xi):\mathbb K_{\zeta}]\le D_S,
 \qquad
 \mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0)\subseteq\mathbb K_{\zeta}(\xi),
 \qquad
 [\mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0):\mathbb K_{\zeta}]\le D_S, \tag{44}
\]
because \(t_0\) is obtained by linear sums of coordinates of \(x_0\).

Each unequal-target test is an existential-realizability problem over
\(\mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0)\) with format
\((N_0,S_0+1,D_0)\), so it generates at most \(A_E\) records.  If a witness
has primitive element \(\upsilon\), then
\[
 [\mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0,\upsilon):\mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0)]\le D_E. \tag{45}
\]
The tower law and (44)--(45) give
\[
 [\mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0,\upsilon):\mathbb K_{\zeta}]
 \le D_SD_E. \tag{46}
\]
Every reported coordinate belongs to the field in (46).  Multiplication by
such a coordinate is a linear operator on a vector space of dimension at
most \(D_SD_E\), so its characteristic polynomial annihilates that
coordinate.  Its minimal polynomial therefore has degree at most
\(D_SD_E\).  Square-free factorization and selection of the correct real root
by Thom signs do not increase degree.  This proves
\(D_{k,\ell}=D_SD_E\) by explicit multiplication of the two sequential
extension degrees.

There are at most \(M_{k,\ell}\) initial calls and at most the same number of
unequal-target calls.  Including the two fixed summary records gives
\[
 2+M_{k,\ell}A_S+M_{k,\ell}A_E
 =R_{k,\ell}, \tag{47}
\]
which bounds all generated records and therefore all retained labeled
outputs.

Let \(Q=k\ell+k^2+\ell+1\).  The explicit counts imply, after changing a
universal constant \(C\),
\[
 M_{k,\ell}\le2^{CQ},\qquad
 N_0\le CQ,\qquad S_0\le CQ,\qquad D_0=4. \tag{48}
\]
The record-count and relative-degree bounds in the effective semialgebraic
sampling lemma, applied separately to the two formats, give
\[
 A_S,D_S,A_E,D_E\le2^{CQ^C}. \tag{49}
\]
Substitution of (48)--(49) into (46)--(47), followed by enlargement of
\(C\), proves
\[
 R_{k,\ell}\le2^{CQ^C},
 \qquad D_{k,\ell}\le2^{CQ^C}. \tag{50}
\]

For arbitrary real input, selected-cell normalization divides only by
\(r_e>0\), and each chart division uses a pivot whose nonzero sign is one of
the chart atoms.  Thus all chart coefficients initially lie in
\(\mathbb K_{\zeta}\).  The chart list is finite, and the cited arithmetic,
order, sign-determination, sampling, and real-root procedures terminate over
the stated oracle field.  This proves relative termination.

Suppose now that all rational input numerators and denominators have binary
length at most \(L\).  Reconstructing deleted simplex coordinates and clearing
only the recorded nonzero denominators in the degree-at-most-four chart atoms
uses at most a quadratic number of elementary products and sums in \(Q\).
The conservative bound
\[
 h_0=64Q^2(L+1) \tag{51}
\]
therefore dominates every resulting integer coefficient length.  Squaring a
recorded nonzero denominator when necessary preserves a strict sign, so this
clearing operation preserves the chart.

The integer-height part of the effective sampling theorem gives
\[
 h_S=\mathsf{Samp}_h(N_0,S_0,D_0,h_0). \tag{52}
\]
The unequal-target coefficients additionally contain \(t_0\), represented
in an extension of degree at most \(D_S\) and height at most \(h_S\).
Application of the existential height bound over that represented extension
gives
\[
 h_E=\mathsf{Exist}_h(N_0,S_0+1,D_0;h_0,h_S,D_S). \tag{53}
\]
Finally, multiplication matrices in dimension at most \(D_SD_E\), followed
by square-free factorization and root isolation, give
\[
 h_F=\mathsf{Flat}_h(D_SD_E,h_S+h_E+1). \tag{54}
\]
This normalization preserves the degree bound (46).  For each of the two
algorithmic stages, the height exponent is at most \(2^{CQ^C}\) by
(48)--(49); the same is true for the finite tower-flattening stage because
\(D_SD_E\le2^{CQ^C}\).  There are only finitely many sequential
substitutions, so their exponents may be absorbed by enlarging \(C\).  Thus
\[
 H_{k,\ell}(L)=\max\{h_S,h_E,h_F\}
 \le \bigl[64Q^2(L+2)\bigr]^{2^{CQ^C}}. \tag{55}
\]
This is the separate rational-height guarantee, not a claim that height is
singly exponential in the alphabet parameter.  Square-free normalization
and rational isolation give the representations claimed in the statement.
All enumerations and rational subroutines are finite, so the rational-input
Turing implementation terminates.  Its decision stages are precisely chart
enumeration, one initial sample, and the one-copy existential refinements;
neither component decomposition nor target projection is required.

Let \(H\) be a compact subset of \(\mathfrak R_{\varepsilon}\); every
uniform assertion below is over \(\zeta\in H\).  Under independent
multinomial sampling, the reduced selected-table coordinates are averages of
bounded categorical vectors.  In design A with estimated margins, the margin
coordinates are averages from an independent sample and
\(n/n_m\to\lambda\in(0,\infty)\).  Therefore a constant \(C_H<\infty\)
exists such that
\[
 \sup_{\zeta\in H}
 E_{\zeta}\|\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta\|_2^2
 \le \frac{C_H}{n}. \tag{56}
\]
The margin summand is zero when margins are known.  Markov's inequality gives
\[
 \sup_{\zeta\in H}P_{\zeta}
 \{\|\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta\|_2>\delta\}
 \le\frac{C_H}{n\delta^2},
 \qquad
 \widehat\zeta_n-\zeta=O_P(n^{-1/2}) \tag{57}
\]
uniformly on \(H\).

The selected-table covariance is
\(\operatorname{diag}(p^-)-p^-p^{-\top}\).  Independence and the relative
sample-size limit add the block
\(\lambda\{\operatorname{diag}(m^-)-m^-m^{-\top}\}\) when margins are
estimated, and no block when they are known.  These are exactly the blocks of
\(\Omega_{\zeta}\).  The multinomial central-limit and delta lemma yields
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta)
 \Rightarrow N(0,\Omega_{\zeta}). \tag{58}
\]
The convergence is uniform on \(H\).  Indeed, from any sequence in \(H\),
compactness extracts a subsequence converging to \(\zeta_\star\).  For each
fixed vector \(u\), bounded categorical summands give the uniform expansion
\[
 E_{\zeta_n}\exp\{iu^{\top}\xi_{n,1}/\sqrt n\}
 =1-\frac{u^{\top}\Omega_{\zeta_n}u}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}). \tag{59}
\]
Multiplication of the selected and independently rescaled margin
characteristic functions, together with \(n/n_m\to\lambda\), proves (58)
along that subsequence.  The subsequence criterion proves uniformity.
Because the covariance formula is polynomial in the cell probabilities,
(57) and continuous mapping also give
\[
 \widehat\Omega_n\xrightarrow{P}\Omega_{\zeta} \tag{60}
\]
uniformly on \(H\).

For every \(\zeta\in H\), the incident set
\[
 \Gamma(\zeta)
 =\{\chi:d_{\chi}(\zeta)=0,
             \ \eta_{\chi}(\zeta)\ge\varepsilon\} \tag{61}
\]
is nonempty.  Distance to a closed set is one-Lipschitz, so each
\(\chi\in\Gamma(\zeta)\) obeys
\[
 d_{\chi}(\widehat\zeta_n)
 \le\|\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta\|_2. \tag{62}
\]
There are finitely many labels and their normalized slack functions have the
continuous extensions required in \(\mathfrak R_{\varepsilon}\).  Compactness
therefore supplies \(\delta_H>0\) such that
\[
 \|\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta\|_2<\delta_H
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \eta_{\chi}(\widehat\zeta_n)\ge\varepsilon/2
 \quad(\chi\in\Gamma(\zeta)). \tag{63}
\]
Since \(t_n=n^{-1/4}\), (57), (62), and (63) show that some incident chart
passes both selector inequalities with probability tending uniformly to one.

Conversely, the closure of each incompatible chart is at distance at least
\(\varepsilon\) from \(\zeta\).  Hence
\[
 d_{\chi}(\widehat\zeta_n)
 \ge\varepsilon-\|\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta\|_2. \tag{64}
\]
On the event in which the last norm is below \(\varepsilon/2\), (64) exceeds
\(t_n\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); no incompatible chart can pass.
The exhaustive atlas certification and lexicographic selection thus imply
\[
 \sup_{\zeta\in H}P_{\zeta}\{\widehat\chi_n=\bot
 \text{ or }\widehat\chi_n\text{ is not incident and first-order
 compatible}\}\longrightarrow0. \tag{65}
\]

On the complementary event, rigidity and first-order compatibility give
\[
 F_{\widehat\chi_n}(\zeta)=\tau,
 \qquad J_{\widehat\chi_n}(\zeta)=J(\zeta), \tag{66}
\]
where \(J(\zeta)\) is the common incident Jacobian.  The twice continuously
differentiable extensions, finite chart set, and compactness yield a common
Hessian bound.  Taylor's theorem, (57), and (66) therefore give
\[
 \widehat\tau_n-\tau
 =J(\zeta)(\widehat\zeta_n-\zeta)+R_n,
 \qquad
 \sqrt n\|R_n\|_2=o_P(1) \tag{67}
\]
uniformly on \(H\).  Combining (58) and (67) proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau)
 \Rightarrow N(0,J(\zeta)\Omega_{\zeta}J(\zeta)^{\top})
 =N(0,V_{\tau}). \tag{68}
\]

Continuity of the derivatives, (57), and (60) show that the raw sandwich
matrix
\[
 \widetilde V_n=
 J_{\widehat\chi_n}(\widehat\zeta_n)\widehat\Omega_n
 J_{\widehat\chi_n}(\widehat\zeta_n)^{\top}
\]
satisfies \(\widetilde V_n\xrightarrow{P}V_{\tau}\) uniformly.  Since
\(\lambda_{\min}(V_{\tau})\ge\varepsilon\), Weyl's inequality gives
\[
 P_{\zeta}\{\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde V_n)>\varepsilon/2\}
 \longrightarrow1 \tag{69}
\]
uniformly.  Thus \(\widehat\gamma_n=1\) with probability tending to one,
and on that event \(\widehat V_n=\widetilde V_n\).  Hence
\[
 \widehat V_n\xrightarrow{P}V_{\tau}. \tag{70}
\]

For any fixed nonzero contrast vector \(h\), the lower eigenvalue condition
and Slutsky's lemma give
\[
 \frac{\sqrt n\,h^{\top}(\widehat\tau_n-\tau)}
      {(h^{\top}\widehat V_nh)^{1/2}}
 \Rightarrow N(0,1), \tag{71}
\]
so the corresponding two-sided scalar Wald interval has asymptotic coverage
\(1-\alpha\).  Likewise,
\[
 n(\widehat\tau_n-\tau)^{\top}\widehat V_n^{-1}
   (\widehat\tau_n-\tau)
 \Rightarrow\chi^2_2. \tag{72}
\]
The true target belongs to \([0,1]^2\), so intersecting the ellipse with that
square does not change its coverage event.  Continuity of the chi-square law
at its displayed quantile proves coverage \(1-\alpha\) for the elliptical
branch, uniformly on \(H\).

Finally, if no chart is certified, the selector definition gives
\(\widehat\chi_n=\bot\).  The total-map definitions then give
\(F_{\bot}=(0,0)\), \(J_{\bot}=0\), and a zero raw sandwich matrix.  It is
not positive definite, so \(\widehat\gamma_n=0\), and the fallback clauses
give identically
\[
 \widehat\tau_n=(0,0),\qquad
 \widehat V_n=I_2,\qquad W_n=[0,1]^2. \tag{73}
\]
The consistency and Wald conclusions used the high-probability event (65),
so none is asserted for this fallback branch.

Let \(q_0\) denote the true observable law, including the independent margin
law in design A when margins are estimated, and set
\(t_0=\tau(\vartheta)\).  Each selected-table count and each applicable
margin count has a binomial marginal law.  Exact two-tail inversion gives its
Clopper--Pearson interval the allocated marginal coverage.  The stated
Bonferroni allocation therefore gives
\[
 P_{q_0}\{q_0\notin C_n\}\le\beta_n. \tag{74}
\]

For a fixed compatible pair \((q,t)\), define the exact nonrandomized upper
tail
\[
 G_{q,t}=P_q\{\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rep}}(t)
                 \ge\Delta_n^{\mathrm{obs}}(t)\}.
\]
It is super-uniform.  To verify this, order the finite support of
\(\Delta_n(t)\).  For \(u\in[0,1]\), let \(d\) be the least support point
whose upper-tail probability is at most \(u\), if it exists.  Then
\(\{G_{q,t}\le u\}\subseteq\{\Delta_n^{\mathrm{obs}}(t)\ge d\}\), so
\[
 P_q\{G_{q,t}\le u\}\le u. \tag{75}
\]
If no such \(d\) exists, the event on the left is empty and the same
inequality holds.

Compatibility gives \(t_0\in\mathcal T(q_0)\).  On
\(\{q_0\in C_n\}\), the supremum in the calibrated value includes \(q_0\),
and hence
\[
 \operatorname{pv}_n(t_0)
 \ge\min\{1,\beta_n+G_{q_0,t_0}\}. \tag{76}
\]
Since \(\beta_n\le\alpha/2<\alpha\), (74)--(76) yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P_{q_0}\{t_0\notin K_n\}
 &\le P_{q_0}\{q_0\notin C_n\}
   +P_{q_0}\{G_{q_0,t_0}\le\alpha-\beta_n\}\\
 &\le\beta_n+(\alpha-\beta_n)=\alpha.
 \end{aligned} \tag{77}
\]
This is a finite-sample pointwise argument.  Applying (77) at every member of
an arbitrary triangular sequence proves the claim near
\(\mathfrak D\), including point-to-set transitions, without a rank, support,
or boundary limit assumption.

For the additional Hausdorff assertion, fix a compact subset satisfying the
stated local-saturation hypotheses.  Positivity and compactness bound all
local multinomial cell probabilities away from zero.  Since eventually
\(\beta_n=n^{-2}\), simultaneous Clopper--Pearson inversion and a union bound
give
\[
 \sup_{q\in C_n}\|q-q_0\|_2
 =O_P\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n}}\right)=o_P(1) \tag{78}
\]
uniformly.  For completeness, if \(x>p\), exponential Markov inequality at
\(\theta=\log\{x(1-p)/(p(1-x))\}\) gives
\[
 P_p(\widehat p\ge x)
 \le e^{-nD(x\Vert p)}
 \le e^{-2n(x-p)^2}; \tag{79}
\]
the last inequality follows because the second derivative of binary
divergence in \(x\) is \(1/\{x(1-x)\}\ge4\), while the divergence and its
first derivative vanish at \(x=p\).  The lower-tail argument is symmetric.
Inversion at tails of order \(n^{-2}\) proves (78).  With probability tending
to one, every law entering the supremum in the definition of \(K_n\) is
therefore inside the common saturated neighborhood, where compatibility
holds and \(t\in\mathcal T(q)\) is equivalent to \(t=F(q)\).

Write \(z\) for reduced observable coordinates and \(\widehat z\) for their
unrestricted multinomial maximum-likelihood estimate.  A third-order Taylor
expansion of the finite multinomial log likelihood, uniform on the positive
compact neighborhood, gives for
\(z-\widehat z=O(n^{-1/2})\)
\[
 2\{\ell_n(\widehat z)-\ell_n(z)\}
 =n(z-\widehat z)^{\top}\Omega_{\zeta}^{-1}
       (z-\widehat z)+o_P(1). \tag{80}
\]
For two samples, independence and \(n/n_m\to\lambda\) give exactly the two
blocks in \(\Omega_{\zeta}\).  The inverse exists in reduced coordinates
because all local cell probabilities are positive.

Let \(J=\partial F(\zeta)/\partial\zeta^{\top}\).  Twice continuous
differentiability gives
\[
 F(z)-F(\widehat z)
 =J(z-\widehat z)+O(\|z-\widehat z\|_2^2). \tag{81}
\]
Strict concavity of the interior multinomial likelihood and compactness give
a positive Kullback--Leibler gap outside the fixed saturated neighborhood.
Thus every constrained maximizer for a bounded root-\(n\) target displacement
is local with probability tending uniformly to one.

Minimize the leading quadratic form in (80) subject to the linearized
constraint in (81).  The Lagrangian first-order condition gives
\[
 z-\widehat z
 =\Omega_{\zeta}J^{\top}
   (J\Omega_{\zeta}J^{\top})^{-1}(t-\widehat\tau_n),
\]
and substitution, with
\(V_{\tau}=J\Omega_{\zeta}J^{\top}\), gives the profile expansion
\[
 \Delta_n(t)
 =n(t-\widehat\tau_n)^{\top}V_{\tau}^{-1}
       (t-\widehat\tau_n)+o_P(1) \tag{82}
\]
uniformly for bounded \(\sqrt n\|t-\widehat\tau_n\|_2\).  The multiplier is
unique because \(\lambda_{\min}(V_{\tau})\ge\varepsilon\).  The same bound
and (80) show that the profile discrepancy diverges uniformly outside a
bounded local target set.

Applying (80)--(82) to independent replicates, uniformly over the shrinking
set in (78), and using the finite-alphabet central limit theorem yields
\[
 \sup_{q\in C_n:\,t=F(q)}
 \left|
 P_q\{\Delta_n^{\mathrm{rep}}(t)\ge\Delta_n^{\mathrm{obs}}(t)\}
 -\overline F_{\chi^2_2}\!\left(
 n(t-\widehat\tau_n)^{\top}\widehat V_n^{-1}
 (t-\widehat\tau_n)\right)
 \right|=o_P(1). \tag{83}
\]
Here covariance consistency is supplied by the separated-Wald theorem.  The
positive definiteness of \(V_{\tau}\) means that \(J\) has row rank two.
Since \(F\) maps a neighborhood into \([0,1]^2\), this full row rank and the
local open-mapping property force \(F(\zeta)\) into the interior of the
square.  Thus truncation by \([0,1]^2\) is locally inactive.

The chi-square distribution is continuous and \(\beta_n=o(1)\).  Equation
(83) therefore sandwiches \(K_n\), with probability tending to one, between
the ellipsoids obtained by changing \(\chi^2_{2,1-\alpha}\) by
\(\pm\delta_n\), for some \(\delta_n=o_P(1)\).  The eigenvalues of
\(\widehat V_n\) are uniformly bounded above and away from zero.  Radial
comparison of these ellipsoids gives
\[
 d_{\mathrm H}(K_n,W_n)
 \le n^{-1/2}O_P(\delta_n)=o_P(n^{-1/2}), \tag{84}
\]
which is the claimed compact-uniform Hausdorff limit.  Without singleton
local saturation, separation, or nonsingularity, steps (80)--(84) need not
hold; the universally valid conclusion then remains only (77).

Positivity of the selected table gives \(v_e(z)>0\) for every cell and every
\(z\).  If \(\mathcal I_e=\{i,j\}\), every point of either cycle fiber
satisfies
\[
 T_e=b_i a_{ei}^{\top}+b_j a_{ej}^{\top},
 \qquad a_{ei}+a_{ej}=v_e. \tag{85}
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{rank}(T_e)\le2\).  A rank exceeding two makes the cycle
fiber empty, while rank zero is impossible because \(T_e\) is positive.

For a rank-two cell, define its normalized columns
\[
 c_{ez}=\frac{T_e(\cdot,z)}{v_e(z)}.
\]
Equation (85) gives
\[
 c_{ez}=\lambda_{ez}b_i+(1-\lambda_{ez})b_j,
 \qquad
 \lambda_{ez}=a_{ei}(z)/v_e(z)\in[0,1]. \tag{86}
\]
Rank two forces \(b_i\ne b_j\).  Conversely, if endpoints on the observed
affine line contain every \(c_{ez}\) in their closed segment, choose a
coordinate \(h_e\) separating them and set
\[
 a_{ei}(z)=v_e(z)
 \frac{c_{ez}(h_e)-b_j(h_e)}{b_i(h_e)-b_j(h_e)},
 \qquad
 a_{ej}(z)=v_e(z)-a_{ei}(z). \tag{87}
\]
The recorded pivot makes the denominator nonzero, and the segment condition
makes both coefficients nonnegative.  The two endpoint orders are exactly
the orientations in the rank-two atlas.  For each \(z\), the positive sum in
(85) permits precisely the three support alternatives: left zero, right
zero, or both positive.  Hence the stated refinements exhaust every
rank-two support face.

For a rank-one cell, the rank-one normal-form lemma proves that the modes
\(\mathrm L,\mathrm R,\mathrm E,\mathrm D\) are disjoint and exhaustive.
In the first two modes the inactive endpoint remains subject to its simplex
and shared-vertex constraints.  Mode \(\mathrm E\) retains every
coordinatewise zero, strict-interior, and upper-endpoint split; mode
\(\mathrm D\) retains its strict convex coefficient.  Thus equal endpoints,
inactive rows, and forced-zero faces are not removed by division or a rank
argument.

Take the product of the four local mode lists and use one common variable
\(b_i\) at the two incidences of response type \(i\).  Fix endpoint and
coefficient support states.  Endpoint equalities and inequalities, affine-line
incidences, segment order, and guarded pivots are polynomial sign atoms; a
remaining finite alternative is retained as a Boolean combination.  A
denominator in (87) is cleared only after its nonzero sign is recorded.
The rank-two atlas, the rank-one normal forms, and (86)--(87) show that every
point of \(\mathcal C_A(T)\) enters some chart.  Conversely, direct
substitution of a chart point into (85), the simplex equations, and the
support constraints proves membership in \(\mathcal C_A(T)\).  Therefore
\[
 \bigcup_{\chi}X_{\chi}=\mathcal C_A(T). \tag{88}
\]

For design B, adjoin a positive projective vector \(\rho\).  At each response
type, the residual-forest theorem proves the exhaustive alternatives: both
incident residuals vanish; exactly one vanishes, which is infeasible; or both
are nonzero and negatively proportional.  In the active case the first
nonzero residual coordinate is a valid lexicographic pivot and its two signs
give a finite refinement.  The positive margin ratios propagate from one
positive scale in each forest component.  If all four links form a cycle,
path consistency is equivalent to its product-one equation.  Positive scales
and normalization give exactly the positive margins.  Finally, an instrument
is relevant exactly when some ordered pair and one of the two signs certify
\[
 q^X_zg(z')-q^X_{z'}g(z)\ne0. \tag{89}
\]
The residual-forest theorem consequently gives the exact finite union
\[
 \bigcup_{\chi}X_{\chi}=\mathcal C_B(T). \tag{90}
\]

The supplied margin does not appear in (88).  The design-A nonemptiness
criterion therefore requires the preliminary test
\[
 \mathcal F_A(p,m)\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 m\in\Delta_{\mathcal E}^{\circ}
 \ \text{and}\ 
 \bigcup_{\chi}X_{\chi}\ne\varnothing. \tag{91}
\]
Thus an invalid supplied margin is rejected before sampling or lifting.  In
design B, (90) and surjectivity of the cycle-to-SCM lift give
\[
 \mathcal F_B(p)\ne\varnothing
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \bigcup_{\chi}X_{\chi}\ne\varnothing. \tag{92}
\]

Assume the applicable union is nonempty.  The target
\[
 \tau_C(b,a)=
 \left(\sum_z a_{11,2}(z),\sum_z a_{00,2}(z)\right) \tag{93}
\]
is polynomial in the chart variables.  Apply the one-sample/all-chart lemma
to (88) or (90), with \(f=\tau_C\).  It samples \(x_0\), fixes
\(t_0=\tau_C(x_0)\), and proves
\[
 \tau_C\!\left(\bigcup_{\chi}X_{\chi}\right)=\{t_0\}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 X_{\chi}\cap\{x:\|\tau_C(x)-t_0\|_2^2>0\}=\varnothing
 \quad\text{for every }\chi. \tag{94}
\]
This is global even when charts are disconnected or lie on different support
faces, because every point is tested against the same fixed \(t_0\).

The initial sample has a real-univariate representation over
\(\mathbb K_{\zeta}\), and (93) places \(t_0\) in its finite real algebraic
coordinate field.  Each refinement is therefore effective over
\(\mathbb K_{\zeta}(t_0)\).  If all are empty, the exact encoding of \(t_0\)
is returned; a rational expression over \(\mathbb K_{\zeta}\) is used only
when actually constructed, and otherwise the real-univariate and Thom data
are retained.  If a refinement is nonempty, sampling returns \(x_1\) with
\(\tau_C(x_1)\ne\tau_C(x_0)\).  Equations (88) or (90) make both points legal
cycle points, and the target-preserving lift produces full SCM twins with
the same observables and, in design A, the same supplied margins.  Each test
has only the one variable block \(x\); \(t_0\) is a fixed algebraic
coefficient.  Thus no generic two-copy classifier or connected-component
description is used, completing the proof.
